title: Removal of Tractor Hydraulic System Components and Parts

lessons.title: Making the hydraulic system safe
lessons.html:
Why hydraulics need special care

The hydraulic system lifts the three-point linkage, works the loader, helps the steering and sometimes the brakes. Oil in the system can be under very high pressure, even after the engine stops. A hose opened under pressure can spray oil into your eyes or through your skin. An implement can drop and crush you.

Steps to make it safe

  1. Park on level ground. Apply the handbrake and chock the wheels.
  2. Lower all implements and the loader bucket to the ground.
  3. Stop the engine and take out the key.
  4. Move each hydraulic control lever back and forth a few times to release pressure.
  5. If the tractor has an accumulator, ask the mechanic to release its pressure as the manual shows.
  6. Let the oil cool. Hot oil can burn you.

Never

  • Never work under a raised implement or loader held up only by hydraulics. Use the safety lock or stands.
  • Never loosen a fitting with the engine running.
  • Never feel for a leak with your hand. Use cardboard.

If oil is injected through your skin, it is an emergency. Go to a doctor straight away and tell them it is a hydraulic injection injury.

Keep it clean

Dirt is the enemy of hydraulics. Clean the outside of fittings, valves and cylinders before you open anything. Have caps and plugs ready for every open hose and port. Use lint-free rags.

Draining oil

Many tractors share one oil for the gearbox and hydraulics. Draining may mean many litres. Use a large clean container. Look at the oil: milky means water, foamy means air, dark and burnt smelling means overheating. Tell the mechanic.

lessons.title: Removing hoses, cylinders, valves and pumps
lessons.html:
Hoses and pipes

  1. Put a drip tray under the fitting.
  2. Label both ends of the hose and the port it came from.
  3. Hold the fitting body with one spanner and undo the nut with another. This stops the pipe twisting.
  4. Cap the hose and plug the port at once.
  5. Check the old hose for cracks, bulges and wear, and tell the mechanic.

Cylinders

Lift cylinders and loader cylinders are heavy.

  • Support the implement or loader arm with stands or blocks before removing the cylinder pins.
  • Support the cylinder with a crane, sling or helper.
  • Remove the hoses and cap them.
  • Remove locking bolts or clips, then drive out the pins with a soft drift. Keep your fingers out of the holes.
  • Lay the cylinder on a clean bench with the ports capped. Do not push the rod in or out with ports open.

Control valves

Valves are made with very small clearances. Handle them carefully:

  • Photograph and label all pipes, wires and levers.
  • Unplug solenoid connectors by pressing the lock tab.
  • Undo mounting bolts and lift the valve out straight.
  • Cap every port and keep the valve upright in a clean box.
  • Never take a valve apart unless the mechanic tells you to.

Pumps

The pump is usually driven by the engine or gearbox. The mechanic will show you which drive parts to remove. Support the pump before taking out the last bolts. Keep the drive coupling and any O-rings with it.

Recording and cleanup

List all parts removed on the job card. Put used oil in the used oil drum and oily rags in the closed bin. Clean spills with absorbent.

Key points

  • Lower everything, stop the engine and release pressure first.
  • Never work under an implement held only by hydraulics.
  • Clean before opening and cap every hose and port at once.
  • Use two spanners on fittings so pipes do not twist.
  • Support heavy cylinders and pumps before removing the last pin or bolt.
